draft.title: Relevant and reliable sources
card: a source that is about your question. A source on petrol prices in Perth does not help with a question on rents in Hobart.
a source you can trust. It comes from an expert or an official body, such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
A reliable source is also recent, so the facts have not gone out of date. It backs its claims with evidence, such as data you can check.
A source can be relevant but not reliable, or reliable but not relevant. Good research needs both.
draft.remember: Relevant fits your question. Reliable can be trusted. Use sources that are both.

a.q: Which source is most reliable for a question on how many people are employed in Australia?
opts: A recent ABS report with its data tables
A post by an anonymous user on a chat forum
A blog by a student who guesses the numbers
A shop advertisement from ten years ago
a.why: The ABS is an official body, and a recent report with data tables gives evidence you can check. The forum post and the blog give no expert or evidence, and the old advertisement is out of date.
a.clue: Look for an official body, recent facts and data.

b.q: Sam is researching how a rise in interest rates affects Australian home buyers. He finds a recent Reserve Bank of Australia report on interest rates in New Zealand. What is the best description of this source?
opts: Reliable, but not relevant to his question
Relevant, but not reliable for his question
Both relevant and reliable for his question
Neither relevant nor reliable for his question
b.why: The Reserve Bank of Australia is an official body and the report is recent, so it is reliable. It is about New Zealand, not Australian home buyers, so it is not relevant. A tempting wrong answer is that a reliable source is always useful, but it must also fit the question.
b.clue: Check whether it is trustworthy, then check whether it matches the question.

a.best: A recent ABS report with its data tables

b.best: Reliable, but not relevant to his question
